t: as it is said, “You shall not steal”. The prohibition “You shall not steal” in the Ten Commandments refers to kidnapping a person, not to stealing money (below 9:1).
for it is given to payment. And one does not receive lashes for a negative commandment that carries an obligation of payment (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2; see also Hilchot Gezelah 1:1).
for the Torah obligated the thief to pay. As explained in the portion Mishpatim (Exodus 21:37-22:3).
or one who steals the money of an idolatrous gentile. See also below 7:8, Hilchot Gezelah 1:2.
any amount at all. Even if it is worth less than a perutah, it is nevertheless forbidden by the Torah to steal it.

therefore an armed robber who stole is not a robber but a thief. A “listes mezuyan” is an armed bandit. Although when he takes by force he is considered a robber, when he steals secretly he is considered a thief (Lechem Mishneh; the Ra'avad had a different text of the Rambam and therefore objected to him).

even if the owners know at the time he steals. Even if the owners saw him stealing and did not intervene because they feared him, since the thief himself acted in a thieving manner he is considered a thief (Yad Peshutah).
a garment. A piece of clothing.
two times its value. Double its worth, and the additional payment is a fine on the thief.

whom the judges condemn shall pay double to his neighbor. “Elohim” is a term for judges, so the fine is paid only when the court obligates the person, and one who obligated himself does not pay double.
and the same applies to all fines, in which one who admits is exempt. See below 3:7, Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 9:6, Hilchot Avadim 5:17.
except for a sheep and an ox. For which he sometimes pays more than double.
and slaughtered it. Slaughtered it (see below 2:8).
if she was a married woman who has nothing to pay with. For basically a woman's property belongs to her husband.

the double payment remains a debt on her, etc.. She returns the stolen item itself to its owners, but the double is treated as a debt whose time for payment will arrive when she has money in her own possession, for example if she is divorced or widowed (compare Hilchot Chovel 4:21).

and a minor who stole, etc.. A minor is exempt from punishment and responsibility for his actions and therefore is exempt from paying even when he grows up, but if the stolen item exists it is returned to its owners (compare Hilchot Chovel 4:20).
the slave. A Canaanite slave, all of whose property belongs to his master.
is exempt from the double payment. He does not pay the double because he has no money of his own.

for a person is not liable for the damages of his slaves even though they are his property, etc.. Unlike his animal, which is his property and for whose damages he is liable because he has the ability to guard it, he is not liable for the damages of his slaves because they have intelligence and can evade his supervision and go and cause damage.
his master. His lord.
let him go and set fire to a stack worth a thousand dinars. In order to make his master pay for it.
if the slave is freed he is liable to pay the double. Since he is responsible for his actions, therefore when he has money of his own he must pay (compare Hilchot Chovel 4:21).
according to the capacity of the minor. According to what he is able to bear.
a force that is accustomed to cause damage. A power that is forewarned to do damage.
and it improved on its own. Without any monetary expense by the thief.
that it gave birth and he sheared it. It bore young while with the thief, or the thief sheared its wool.

and if after the owners' despair it gave birth and he sheared it, he pays as at the time of the theft. By strict law, the increase belongs to the one from whom it was stolen, since the animal is his; but the Sages ordained that if the owners despaired of the stolen item, any increase that comes afterward remains with the thief. This is because of the “enactment for penitents”: the Sages feared that thieves would refrain from repenting if they were required to return the increase that arose in their possession (Hilchot Gezelah 2:2).

if he spent money on it and it improved... the increase belongs to the thief even before despair. Some explained that this law too is because of the enactment for penitents, that for an increase on which he spent money they ordained that he acquires it even before despair (Or Sameach and others; and see Even ha-Azel, Nizkei Mamon 7:12, who explained otherwise; and compare Hilchot Gezelah 2:9).
or they deduct it from the double. They subtract the value of the increase from the double payment.
returns to its owners, whether before despair or after despair, etc.. Since despair alone does not effect acquisition.
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 11.

if the stolen item changed in the thief's hands, he acquired it. Since it changed, he acquired it and is liable to pay only its value (details of the laws of acquiring a stolen item through change appear in Hilchot Gezelah chapter 2).
and he acquired its increase. What it improved after the change, since it is his.
even before despair. For change effects acquisition even without despair.
and he pays only its value. According to its value at the time of the theft (see Hilchot Gezelah 2:1).
a lean animal. A thin animal.
as at the time of the theft. According to its value at the time of the theft.
or the payments of four and five. If he slaughtered or sold it.
he stole a lamb and it became a ram. He stole a sheep close to its birth and it stayed with him until it grew and became a ram.

a change occurred in his hands and he acquired it, etc.. The transition from lamb to ram and from calf to ox is considered a change; therefore the thief acquires the animal, and if he slaughtered or sold it he does not need to pay the payments of four and five.

he pays the principal as at the time of the theft and the double or four-and-five payments as at the time of standing trial. The basic rule is that if the stolen item no longer exists he pays the principal according to its value at the time of the theft, and the fine payments according to the time of standing trial (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 65a). But there are exceptions to this rule, as explained here.

if he slaughtered... he pays the double or four-and-five payments as at the time of standing trial. And in this case he pays the principal too according to the time of standing trial, because he destroyed the animal with his own hands (Maggid Mishneh, based on the Rif).

and if the animal died or the vessel was lost on its own, he pays the double payment as at the time of the theft. And in this case he does not pay as at the time of standing trial, since the animal rose in value and he did not destroy it with his hands.
he diminished it. It was damaged but not broken.
they do not assess the diminution for him. He cannot return the broken vessel and pay the decrease in its value plus the addition of the double.

and if the owners wish to take the broken vessel and he pays them the diminution and the double, they listen to them. And the thief did not acquire the vessel when it was diminished or broken (the commentators on the Rambam found it difficult why breaking is not considered a change through which the thief would acquire the vessel; see Gra, Choshen Mishpat 354, note 13, and Ketzot ha-Choshen there, note 3; and Yad Peshutah wrote, based on Hilchot Gezelah 2:15, that this is an enactment made for the owners, that in this case the thief does not acquire the item even though a change was made in it).

even though the buyer did not acquire... he pays the payments of four and five. Even though the act of sale was ineffective and the animal returns by itself to its owners, he nevertheless pays four and five (this refers only to the case where he stole and sold, not where he stole and slaughtered, in which case the thief acquires the animal through a change of act, as explained below, halakhah 18).

and needless to say if he slaughtered or sold after despair... for his actions were effective and the buyer acquired. When he sold the animal after despair the buyer acquired it, since a stolen item is acquired through despair and change of ownership (“shinui reshut”; below 5:3, Hilchot Gezelah 2:3). And if in a sale without despair, where the animal returns to the owners, he pays four and five, all the more so if there was despair and it does not return to the owners that he pays four and five.
from the thief. From the thief himself.
and if he slaughtered and sold. The second thief.

for the law of this animal is to return as it is to the owners, and the thief did not acquire it. The first thief did not acquire it, since despair alone does not effect acquisition and had it been with him it would have returned to the owners; and since it is not his, one who steals from him is exempt from paying him.
nor does he have to pay the owners. He is not obligated to pay the original owners either.
because he did not steal from their possession. And the double payment is stated in the Torah only regarding one who steals from the owners' possession (see Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 69b).
and another thief came and stole the slaughtered animal. The animal the first thief slaughtered.
for he acquired it through a change of act. For it was an animal and now there is meat here.
through a change of act. A change made in the body of the stolen item.
and the first thief pays the payments of four and five. To the owners, since he became obligated to pay at the time of the slaughter.
the first pays the payments of four and five. To the original owners, like any thief who stole and sold.
and the second thief pays the double payments. To the one who bought from the thief, since he acquired it through despair and change of ownership.
and if the owners did not despair. In which case the stolen item remained in their ownership even after the sale and the buyer did not acquire it.
the last one pays only the principal. Since he did not steal from the owners' house he is exempt from fine payments (as above, halakhah 17).
consecrated property. Property that belongs to the Temple.
one who steals consecrated property pays only the principal. See also Hilchot Terumot 10:24.
to his neighbor. A Jew.
and likewise one who steals sacrificial animals from their owners' house. Property consecrated for offerings, and because of the theft he cannot offer them.
whether the most holy offerings. Offerings from which the owners do not eat, such as the burnt offering and the sin offering.

or lesser holy offerings. Offerings from which the owners do eat, such as peace offerings. Even though the owners have a right to eat them, they are nonetheless consecrated and one is not liable for the double on them.
or offerings for which the owners are not liable for their replacement. That he is not obligated to offer another offering in place of this one that was stolen.
or offerings for which the owners are liable for their replacement. That he is obligated to offer another offering in place of this one that was stolen, and the theft caused him a monetary loss.

as it is said, “and it was stolen from the man's house,” and not from the house of the Temple. Although the law of theft from consecrated property is learned from the verse “his neighbor,” here there is a novel point that he is exempt even if the one who consecrated has a claim against the thief for preventing him from offering the sacrifice, so a further source is needed (Rash"sh, Bava Kamma 63a; Chiddushei Ha-Griz, Bekhorot 11a). Some explained that the novelty is that he is exempt even when the consecrated property was with another person when it was stolen (Ben Yedid and others).
as it is said, “for an ox, etc.”. Regarding the double payment.
were compared. They were made equivalent to them in halakhic terms.
“and you shall inherit them”. Said regarding slaves, so Scripture treats them as inheritance and as land.
and documents, their body is not money. The value of a document does not derive from the value of the paper but from what is written on it.
a firstborn donkey. The firstborn of a donkey; for it to belong to its owner and be permitted for benefit it must be redeemed with a sheep given to the priest (Hilchot Bikkurim 12:1-2).
it is fit to be his after it is redeemed. Therefore it is within his property for which the thief is liable for fine payments.
his tevel. Produce that is obligated in tithes and is forbidden to eat before they are separated.
he pays him the value of his tevel. Although now the produce is forbidden to eat, it is destined to be permitted to him after he separates the tithes.
its forbidden fat. The animal's fat that is forbidden to eat.
he pays him the value of its forbidden fat. Since the fat is permitted for benefit and he can make use of it (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 8:16).
from its owners, the Israelites who separated it. And who are about to give it to a priest.

and the benefit of giving is not money. The benefit one can receive for giving terumah to a particular priest is not considered money (see also Hilchot Ishut 5:6, Hilchot Terumot 12:15). And if he stole terumah from a priest to whom the terumah belongs, he pays him the double payments (Hilchot Terumot 10:23).
and afterward he consecrated. The animal he slaughtered or sold.
he pays the payments of four and five. Since he became liable for fine payments to the owners while it was still in his possession.
and if he consecrated and afterward slaughtered or sold. So he slaughtered or sold a consecrated animal.
even though he consecrated it as lesser holy offerings, etc.. Even though the one who consecrated has a right to eat its meat, the animal is nonetheless considered to be in the Temple's possession.
in what case does this apply. That he can consecrate the animal he stole, even though a person cannot consecrate something that is not his (Hilchot Arachin va-Charamin 6:24).

when he consecrated after despair. Although a stolen item is not acquired by despair alone but also requires a change of ownership (see below 5:2-3), when he consecrates the animal after despair the consecration takes effect. As to the reason, some wrote that the consecration counts as a change of ownership that acquires together with the despair (Meiri and other early authorities on Bava Kamma 67a). Others wrote that there is a special enactment that consecration takes effect in this case (see Responsa Oneg Yom Tov, no. 29).
and afterward his father died. And he and his brother inherited his property, including the right to receive the theft payments.
he pays the payments of four and five. He pays his brother his proportionate share of the theft payments and acquires his own share (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 7:2).

and if his father died and afterward he slaughtered or sold... he does not pay the payments of four and five. For at the time he slaughtered or sold he had already acquired part of the stolen item, and he is liable for four and five only if the entire animal is forbidden to him by slaughter or sale (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 72a; and see below halakhah 13).

it is not consecrated because it is not in their possession, even though they have not despaired. The owners cannot consecrate it, because a person can consecrate only what is both his and in his possession (see Hilchot Arachin va-Charamin 6:22-24).
he pays the payments of four and five. Since the consecration did not take effect and the animal is still in the owners' possession.
and it became an unfit carcass in his hands. A disqualification occurred in the slaughter, and the animal became a nevelah, forbidden to eat.
and one who wrings the neck or one who uproots. Killings that are not slaughter.
he pays only the double payments. For the slaughtering for which one is liable for four and five is valid slaughter.
but if he slaughtered. Valid slaughter.
for medicine. To give some of it to a sick person or to prepare medicine from it.
or for dogs. To give it to dogs to eat.
or it was found to be a treifah. It became clear that it had an illness or defect or the like that forbids eating it, but the slaughter itself was valid.
or he slaughtered it in the Temple courtyard. In the Temple, where it is forbidden to slaughter (see Hilchot Shechitah 2:1-2).
even though unconsecrated animals slaughtered in the courtyard are forbidden for benefit. And his slaughter did not help to make it permitted for eating.
since their prohibition is only rabbinic. Mi-derabbanan; but by Torah law his slaughter is valid and has the status of slaughter.
a hybrid born of a sheep and another species. A cross of a sheep or goat with a wild animal (Kiryat Melech, based on Tosefta Bava Kamma 7:5).
one with a missing foot. Lacking a leg.
one with a missing hand. Lacking a foreleg.
blind. Sightless.
a jointly owned animal. An animal that belongs to more than one person.

and gave it to another as a gift. Even though he received nothing in return he is liable, because he removed it from his possession (Chiddushei Rabbi Meir Simchah, Bava Kamma 79a; and see Or ha-Chaim, Exodus 23:3). Some explain that presumably he received some compensation for the gift he gave (Yad Peshutah).

or gave it to another to slaughter and he slaughtered, etc.. Even though another person sold and slaughtered on his behalf, and in principle the rule is that there is no agent for a transgression and the principal is not liable for a transgression the agent committed for him, but the agent is responsible for his actions, regarding four and five the Sages learned from the verse that there is an agent for a transgression and the act is attributed to the thief (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 79a).
he stole and sold on credit. He sold it on credit and has not yet received its price.
he stole and exchanged. For something else.
he stole and paid off his credit. He paid the seller for what the seller had sold him on credit.
engagement gifts. Gifts that a groom sends to his betrothed.
and transferred it to the buyer after thirty days. He stipulated at the time of the transaction that it would take effect only after thirty days.
and within thirty days the thief was identified. The thief was found before the sale was completed.
he pays only the double. Since he was caught before the sale took effect.

if he retained in it something that is permitted with it by slaughter, he is exempt from the payments of four and five. Because the Sages learned that liability for sale is similar to slaughter, so all the parts that slaughter permits must be included in the sale (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 78b).
or he sold it except for its labor. He sold the animal itself while retaining for himself the right to have it do work.
or he sold it except for thirty days. He kept for himself a right of use of it for thirty days.

he stole and cut off from it a limb, etc.. In these cases there is doubt whether it counts as a complete sale for which one is liable for four and five payments, and because of the doubt one does not extract money from one who is in possession of it. But if the one robbed seized the thief's property, they do not take it from him, since he is now the one in possession.
he sold it and had a partnership in it. He was a partner in the animal.
exempt from the payments of four and five. Because he is liable for four and five only if the entire animal is forbidden to him by slaughter or sale.
and one of them slaughtered or sold with his fellow's knowledge. So he is like his agent (and see above, halakhah 10).

and if he did it without his fellow's knowledge, they are exempt from the payments of four and five. For the liability of four and five applies only when everyone who stole as a partner also participated in the sale and slaughter.

go give him what... exempt from the payments of four and five. Since his case has already been decided, he is no longer in the status of a thief but of one convicted in court, and the stolen item is like a deposit until he returns it to its owner.

if they said to him, “You are obligated to give him... he is liable for the payments of four and five”. Because this is a statement of principle and not a verdict, so he did not leave the status of a thief (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 7:6).

since the stolen item is still in their possession, he is exempt from the double, etc.. A person does not become a thief merely by concealing his fellow's property, but only if he removed it from his possession: either by an act of acquisition or by actually taking it out of the owners' possession (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 7:6, and below 3:2).
he lifted the stolen item. He picked it up and thereby effected the acquisition of hagbahah (for the acquisition of lifting acquires even in the owner's domain; Hilchot Mechirah 4:3).
he stole a lamb from the pen. He took it from the pen without the owners' knowledge.
and he was pulling it and going out... exempt. For the acquisition of meshichah (pulling) is not effective in the owners' domain, and the lamb is still in their possession.
he placed it there in the owners' house. If before taking the lamb out of the owners' domain the thief gave it to another person to take.
for his firstborn son's redemption. As payment to a priest for the redemption of his firstborn son.
and to his creditor. As payment of a debt.
or to an unpaid guardian, etc.. The thief gave it to another person to take the lamb out and guard it for him.

the guardian is liable, etc.. If he knew that the lamb did not belong to the thief who gave it to him, then he is the one who actually carried out the theft and is liable for it, and the first is exempt since he did not remove it from the owner's domain (Maggid Mishneh).
the flock was in the forest. Outside the owners' domain, where the acquisition of meshichah is effective (see Hilchot Mechirah 2:5).

once he struck the animal and hid it among the trees and wood, etc.. Hakkashah is striking the animal so that it goes, and it has the law of meshichah; and since he also hid it from the owners he became a thief.

he stole within the owners' domain, and after they learned that it was stolen he took it out and slaughtered or sold it outside their domain. Even though when he took it out of their domain they knew about it and it was not done in secret, it is still theft.

or he stole and took it outside their domain and slaughtered or sold it in their domain. Even though he slaughtered or sold it in their domain, he is liable because he became a thief when he took it out, and he has the status of a thief until he returns it to the owners properly.
we already explained in Hilchot Na'arah. Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 1:11-14.
he does not pay even though he was inadvertent, etc.. Even though he is not actually put to death, he is exempt from the payments when this transgression carries a death penalty from the court.
if he was inadvertent or was not warned. And therefore he does not receive lashes.
he pays and does not receive lashes. For a transgression carrying lashes and payments exempts from payment only when he actually receives lashes.
at once. Simultaneously.
he receives lashes and pays and dies. He receives lashes and pays, or pays and dies.

from the beginning of four to the end of four. A distance of four cubits in the public domain; one who throws an object a distance of four cubits in the public domain on the Sabbath is liable to death for the labor of carrying out (Hilchot Shabbat 12:10).
while walking. While in motion, and he is liable to pay for what he damaged, except that here he became liable to pay while performing a labor on the Sabbath.
or he set fire to his fellow's stack on the Sabbath. And he is liable to death for the kindling (see there 12:1).
a purse. A wallet.

until he took it out of the owners' domain. And a thief becomes liable to pay only if he took the stolen item out of the owners' domain (above 2:16), and at that same moment he also became liable for carrying from domain to domain (Hilchot Shabbat 12:8).
and he lost it. For if he had not lost it he would have been required to return it, and he would have been exempt only from paying the double, for which he became liable because of the carrying out.
and he lifted it there in the private domain. And he became a thief (above 2:16).
on a festival. For the punishment for labor on it is lashes.
and they warned him. For without warning he is not liable to lashes.
on Yom Kippur. For the punishment for labor on it is karet and lashes, and the lashes exempt him from payment (but the punishment of karet does not exempt from payment).
but if they did not warn him. And he is exempt from lashes.
a thief who slaughtered on the Sabbath or for idolatry. And he is liable to the court's death penalty for the slaughter (see Hilchot Shabbat 11:1, Hilchot Avodah Zarah 3:1-3).
as we have explained. Above, halakhah 1.

he had a borrowed cow with him and slaughtered it on the Sabbath by way of theft. If he stole and slaughtered at one time, for example he slaughtered it for himself, he acquired it as a thief through the slaughter, and became liable at the same moment both to death and to payments (Merkevet ha-Mishneh; and see Radbaz, who explained otherwise).

he is exempt even from the double. Some explained that this means the principal and the double, and he is exempt from the principal too (Lechem Mishneh, Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 1:5). Others explained that he is exempt only from the double but pays the principal, because the obligation of the principal arises from his having undertaken to return it at the time of the loan, not from his having slaughtered it, and only the fine payments depend on his having slaughtered it (Shach, Choshen Mishpat 354, note 6, and Merkevet ha-Mishneh).

and if there is no theft there is no slaughter and no sale. If he is exempt from payment for the theft itself he is also not liable for four and five (see Shitah Mekubbetzet, Ketubot 34b, on why this reasoning is needed, since apparently he is exempt from four and five because he slaughtered on the Sabbath).
for there is no death in a sale. There is no death penalty for this act.
and if a labor was performed on the Sabbath at the time of the sale. If the transaction involves performing a labor, he is exempt from the fine payment for the sale.

how so? For example, he did not transfer it to him until it rested in the buyer's courtyard, etc.. For the labor of carrying out he is liable only if he lifted the object, moved it to another domain, and set it down there. Therefore, in a case where they expressly agreed that the transaction would not take effect until the stolen item rested in the buyer's courtyard, and the thief carried it to the buyer's courtyard and set it down there, both the sale and the labor of carrying out were completed simultaneously with the setting down.
he appointed an agent. The thief appointed an agent to slaughter the stolen item.

the thief is liable for the payments of four and five, for this thief did not commit a capital transgression. Even though the slaughter made the agent liable to death, the agent's death liability does not exempt the thief from payment, since the exemption from payment applies only when one person became liable for both.
and we have already explained. Above 2:10.
whether others testified. Two other witnesses.
and one witness testifies that he slaughtered or sold. And money is not extracted without two witnesses.
as we have explained. Above 1:5.
before a court. Before three judges.
and in a court. In a place designated for judgment.
exempt. For only such an admission counts as admission in court, and only regarding it is it said that one who admits to a fine is exempt.
and afterward witnesses came. And testified that he is liable.
for he obligated himself for the principal before witnesses came. And since he obligated himself for the principal he is exempt from the double, even if afterward witnesses came that he stole.
and witnesses came that he stole. And he became liable to pay principal and double.

because he first exempted himself from everything. Since he did not admit to the theft itself but only to an obligation that branches out from it, the admission is not considered a complete admission, and therefore he is liable if witnesses afterward come regarding it (Even ha-Azel, Nizkei Mamon 2:8).
he pays the one he denied. For his admission exempts him only in relation to the one to whom he admitted.

if no movable property is found for him, the court goes down to his lands. They collect from his land. But as long as he has movable property they do not collect land from him (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 8:10).
they sell him. To be a slave for six years (below, halakhah 14).
his price. What the buyer paid for him.
but not the woman. A woman who stole and has nothing to pay with.
from the tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
and the thief is sold only for the principal, etc.. The thief is sold only if he cannot pay the principal; but if he paid the principal he is not sold, even if he cannot pay the fine payments.
until he becomes wealthy. And can pay his debt (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 2:1).
he stole from a gentile or from consecrated property. For one does not pay them the double but only the principal (above 2:1).
until he goes free in the seventh year. At the beginning of the seventh year from the day he was sold (Hilchot Avadim 2:2).
the thief was worth a hundred and one. And the stolen goods are worth a hundred.
if he stole for a second. If he stole from another person and not from the one he had already stolen from.
all of them are partners in him. All have a share in his sale, so they assess his value relative to all the thefts together, and if he is not worth more than they, he is sold.
partners who stole as one. Who stole by a joint act.

they divide it among themselves into thirds, etc.. They divide the payment of the principal according to the number of thieves, and if they cannot pay, they assess each one's value only relative to what he must pay, and not relative to the total value of the theft.

if he swore. A guardian who claims that the deposit was stolen must swear the guardians' oath that it was stolen from him and that he was not negligent in guarding it (Hilchot Sechirut 1:2, and see Hilchot She'elah 6:1 for what this oath includes).
for he himself is like a thief. Since he claimed it was stolen from him and he himself took it.

and he does not bring a guilt offering on the basis of witnesses regarding his oath. A guardian who makes a false claim that exempts him from paying for the deposit and afterward admits must bring a guilt offering and pay the principal plus a fifth (Hilchot Shevuot 1:8-9, Hilchot Shegagot 9:7, Hilchot Gezelah 7:1). This obligation applies only when he admits that he lied; but if witnesses testified that he lied and he stands by his claim, he does not bring a guilt offering and a fifth (Hilchot Gezelah 7:8).

and he does not bring a fifth. When witnesses testified that he lied and the guardian became liable for the double, even if he afterward admitted (in which case he becomes liable for a guilt offering), he does not pay a fifth (Yad Peshutah).
for the fifth is not paid together with the double. The Sages learned from the verse that he is liable for a fifth only when he is liable for the principal and not when he is liable for the double.
and if witnesses came before he swore, he pays only the principal. For the double liability of a guardian applies only when he swore falsely.
if he laid a hand on it. Took it from its place in order to take it for himself.

for once he laid a hand on it he became liable for it and acquired it. When a guardian lays a hand on a deposit he becomes a robber and is liable for it (Hilchot Gezelah 3:11), and for this reason he is not considered a thief and is exempt from the double.
and likewise one who claims loss of a deposit and swore. In this case he does not pay the double if there are witnesses that he lied, for one is liable for the double only on a claim of theft.
and afterward witnesses came. That the deposit was with him at the time of the oaths.
exempt from the double. Even for the second oath.

for the deposit already left the owners' hands through the first oath. When he swore that it was lost and did not return it, he is treated as a robber and is no longer in the status of a guardian (Even ha-Azel).
one who makes a claim of theft regarding a lost item. He found a lost item and afterward swore to the one who lost it that it had been stolen from him.

for it is said, “for any lost item”. This verse is stated regarding a guardian who swears falsely and becomes liable to pay double, and from the phrase “for any lost item” the Sages learned that a guardian of a lost item is also included in this law.
an armed bandit. An armed robber.
for he is under duress and exempt. Though this is a claim of theft, unlike ordinary theft its law is that of an unavoidable accident.
for a guardian of a lost item is like a paid guardian. Who is liable for ordinary theft and exempt only for an unavoidable accident.
as will be explained. Hilchot Gezelah va-Avedah 13:10.
and afterward witnesses came that it was in his possession. And he became liable for the double and also must return the deposit, and meanwhile he guards it.

he is liable for the double on each and every claim. For each time witnesses came and testified that he lied he returned to the status of a guardian until he returns the deposit, and consequently he becomes liable again for the double if he claimed it was stolen and swore falsely (unlike above, halakhah 3, where he is not liable for the double for the second oath, since no witnesses came between the oaths and he remained a robber, who has no double liability; Even ha-Azel).
and five on the principal. Another five by virtue of the principal.
and witnesses came that it was not stolen. And he became liable for the double for his first oath.

and he himself admitted that it was not lost. Ordinarily, when one swore falsely on a claim of loss that exempts him from payment and then returned and admitted, he must pay the principal plus a fifth (see above, halakhah 1, in the explanation).

for the money that obligates him for the double exempts him from the fifth. The Sages learned from the verse that he does not pay a fifth when he is already liable for the double for the same deposit, even though the liability for the double and the fifth arises from different oaths.
he handed his ox over to two. To guard it.

and if the owner of the deposit seized the double, they do not take it from his hand. Since the first one who admitted became liable to pay a fifth, there is doubt whether the second is exempt from the double because one does not pay both double and a fifth on the same deposit, or whether he is liable for the double because he is not the one paying the fifth, but someone else. Because of the doubt the second guardian is not held liable for the double, but if the owner of the deposit seized it himself they do not take it from his hand, since he is now the one in possession and one does not take from him on account of a doubt (see above 2:12, in the explanation; and see Or Sameach, Even ha-Azel, and Yad Peshutah on why one does not say that the second guardian pays the double and the first is exempt from the fifth on account of the doubt).
the thief was identified. It became known who the thief was.
if the guardian truly swore when he claimed it was stolen. And there was no flaw in his oath.

the thief is exempt from the double through his admission to the guardian. Since the guardian was shown to be trustworthy when he swore, the owner of the deposit agrees that he sue the thief in his place, and therefore the thief's admission is valid and exempts him from fine payments as one who admits to a fine (Rashi, Bava Kamma 108b).

and if he swore falsely. If there was falsehood in his oath, for example he swore that it was stolen from him in one way and it was discovered that it was indeed stolen from him but in another way (Meiri, ibid. 108a).

they do not extract the double from the thief. For it is doubtful whether in such a case the owner of the deposit agrees that the guardian sue the thief in his place, and therefore it is doubtful whether the thief is exempt from the fine when he admitted.
and if the owners seized the double, they do not take it from their hand. As above, halakhah 7.
the owners sued the guardian and he paid, and afterward the thief was identified. In this case the double payments go to the guardian (Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 8:1).

they do not extract the double from the thief. For it is doubtful whether the owners can sue the thief or only the guardian can sue him, and therefore it is doubtful whether the thief is exempt from the fine when he admitted to them.
and so too regarding the payments of, etc.. For it is doubtful whether the thief is exempt from them when he admitted to the owners.
even though he gave it to him when he was a minor and he sued him when he was an adult. And he made a claim of theft when the depositor was already an adult.
“if a man gives”. From which it follows that the law of one who makes a claim of theft applies only to one who deposited when he was an “ish,” meaning an adult.
and the giving and the suing must both be as an adult. It is not enough that he sued after he grew up.
a guardian who stole from his own possession, for example he stole a lamb from the flock. That he took it for himself (Kesef Mishneh).
and a sela from a purse that was deposited with him. A coin from a wallet given to him to guard.

and even though he returned the sela to its place... he is liable for its responsibility. If the item is lost he must pay the owners, and he does not have the status of a guardian who is exempt in cases of unavoidable accident and the like.

for his guardianship has ended. From the moment he stole he is no longer in the status of a guardian, and therefore it is not enough for him to return it to the place where he was guarding it; he must inform the owners.
until he counts his money. And the owners know that the sela has returned to their possession (compare Hilchot Gezelah 1:8).
and found the count complete. Found that the count was complete as it had been at first.

for he taught it a different way from the way of the rest of the flock in this herd. The lamb became accustomed to walking differently from the rest of the flock while it was with the thief, and the owners need to know that it was stolen and returned so as to watch it more than the rest of the flock.
and it is a great sin, etc.. And he also cannot repent fully for it, because he does not know to whom to return the stolen item (Hilchot Teshuvah 4:3).
a buyer. A purchaser.
and of this it is said, “whoever shares with a thief hates his own soul”. For he brings evil on himself.

one who steals and sells, and the owners have not despaired... the item returns to its owners. Since the owners did not despair, the stolen item still belongs to them and must be returned to them, for theft and robbery are acquired only through the combination of despair and change of ownership (see the next halakhah).

and the owners give the buyer the money he paid the thief, because of the enactment for the market. Although by strict law the owners need not pay the buyer, and the thief must return his money to him, the Sages ordained that the owners pay the buyer so that people not refrain from buying from one another out of fear that it will turn out the item is stolen and be taken from them, and they will also lose what they paid.
and the owners go back and take legal action against the thief. And he pays them what they paid the buyer.
and if he is a notorious thief, they did not make the enactment for the market for him. For there is no reason to protect one who buys from him.

the buyer acquired it through despair and change of possession. Through the owner's despair and the change of possession, the stolen object is acquired by the buyer (see also above 1:16, Hilchot Gezelah 2:3).

rather he gives them the money, if he bought from a notorious thief. Since he was supposed to return the stolen item to the owners and himself collect from the thief what he paid, when he bought it through despair and change of possession he is indeed released from returning the item itself, but he must pay its value to the owners and collect the money from the thief.

when the buyer takes the matter to court against the householder. When he bought from a thief who is not notorious, and the householder whose property was stolen pays the buyer what he paid for the stolen item.
the merchant swears... and collects from the owners. Since the buyer is the one holding the stolen item (see 'halakhah leMoshe').
the merchant. The one who bought from the thief.
swears while holding an object. While holding a Torah scroll (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8, and see there 11:11).
by rabbinic enactment. By enactment of the Sages and not from the Torah.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot To'en veNit'an 1:2.
when the buyer takes the matter to court against the thief. When he bought from a notorious thief and returned the stolen item to the owners without compensation.
the merchant swears. How much he paid.

because he is suspected regarding oaths. The thief should swear regarding his claim, since he is the one holding the money the buyer comes to take from him; but since a thief is suspected of swearing falsely, the oath passes to the buyer, who swears and collects (see Hilchot To'en veNit'an 2:4).
he stole and paid his debt; he stole and paid for what he bought on credit. The thief gave the stolen item to a lender in payment of a debt, or as payment for what he bought on credit.

this does not fall under the enactment for the market. There is no concern that people will refrain from lending or from selling on credit, since the loan or the credit was not given on the understanding that he would give specifically what he stole (Bavli Bava Kamma 115a).

a pledge of stolen goods etc.. If he gave the stolen item to a lender as a pledge to secure repayment, the enactment for the market applies, since the lender lent him against the pledge and this is like a sale, even if he lent more than the pledge is worth and the pledge cannot secure full repayment (see Levush, Choshen Mishpat 356:7).
unless he was a notorious thief, as we have explained. In which case he returns the stolen item to the owners without compensation and goes back to collect his money from the thief (above 5:2).

he collects the money, whether he bought from him something worth one hundred for two hundred etc.. Even if he paid the thief double the value of the stolen item, the owner pays him what he paid and not only the value of the item, since if he paid him less than what he paid there is also concern for harm to commerce.
as we have explained. Above 5:2.
he owed the thief etc.. The thief owed a person one hundred zuz, stole and paid his debt, and afterwards the lender lent him another hundred zuz.

and they say to him etc.. The court tells the lender to return the stolen item to the owners without compensation and to claim from the thief himself, since he originally lent to the thief without security, so the second loan too was not made merely because he received the stolen item in payment of the first debt, but because he relied on the thief to pay his debt. Therefore he is treated like anyone who is paid a debt with stolen goods, and not like one who lent and received the stolen item as a pledge.
he bought from a thief who is not notorious. In which case the owner pays the buyer.
the owner of the stolen item gives the last one one hundred and twenty and takes his stolen item. As explained above 5:7, he gives the buyer what he paid the thief.
and the owner goes back and takes twenty etc.. The owner collects from each of those involved in the sale the profit he made on the stolen item.

and if he is a notorious thief. In which case the law is that the owner takes the stolen item from the buyer and the buyer must take the thief to court (above 5:2; the Derishah wrote that this is how the Raavad explains the Rambam, but some explained the Rambam to mean that the owner pays the buyer since he did not buy from the notorious thief; see Maggid Mishneh).

he takes the one hundred and twenty from the merchant who bought from the thief. He takes from the seller who bought from the thief the one hundred and twenty he paid him, and the seller claims from the thief the hundred he paid him.
all these rulings apply before despair, as we have explained. Above halakhot 2-3. For if he despaired, the stolen item does not return to the owner, and the thief pays the owner its value.
and a reputation for theft arose in the city. It became known that things had been stolen from his house.

or he was in the habit of selling his utensils, of the kind that are made to be lent and rented etc.. Even if the claimant is in the habit of selling his utensils, if these are items meant for renting and lending, the householder is believed when he claims they were stolen from him, because he could have claimed that he lent or rented them to him. All this is on condition that a reputation for theft arose; otherwise the item is deemed to belong to whoever holds it now (Maggid Mishneh, based on Hilchot To'en veNit'an 8:5-6, and see Piskim veShitot).
the one who holds them swears, while holding an object, how much he paid. As above 5:4.
and his utensils were identified. Witnesses identified his items in the defendant's possession.

but if people came and lodged in his house... he is believed. Even if the owner is someone who is in the habit of selling his belongings and these are utensils not made for lending and renting, in this case the circumstances show that these items were stolen from him, and therefore he is believed.
a tunnel dug in. A dug-out opening or breach through which one can steal.
and everyone says. Those who were present there.
a thief who has been established and become known. Who is known to have already stolen several times and has become known as a thief.
hidden for him under his wings. Hidden under the folds of his garment.

even though the householder was there. Although the householder was present, which seemingly is proof that the one carrying out the utensils did not steal from him but bought from him, nevertheless the householder is believed since the one carrying them out is both established as a thief and carried the utensils out like a thief (and see Hilchot Gezelah 4:12, that if he entered the house not in the presence of the householder he is presumed a robber, and the householder is believed to claim that he stole from him without need of an additional condition).

and if this person is not an established thief, the householder is not believed. In claiming that he stole from him; but if he claimed that he lent them to him, he is believed (Hilchot To'en veNit'an 9:4).

the oath of hesset. An oath enacted by the Sages of the Talmud, imposed on one who denies his fellow's entire claim, and it does not involve holding an object (Hilchot Shevuot 11:7, 11:13, Hilchot To'en veNit'an 1:3).
to buy. To purchase.
most of that kind of item is stolen. Most of the merchandise of this type is stolen.
shepherds. Who keep other people's animals in their possession.

one may buy milk and cheese from them in the wilderness but not in a settled area. The milk and cheese in the wilderness are not normally brought by the owners from there, and the shepherd is permitted to sell them. But the milk and cheese in the city are usually brought to the owners.
fleeces. Bundles of shorn wool.
for it is not presumed that he steals a large amount. Since he sells large quantities relative to the flock, he is not presumed to be a thief, because their absence would be noticed.
wood. Which may have been taken from the garden.
and the balance. A weighing instrument.
noise. Publicity.
and one buys from the garden entrance. An additional condition for buying from them is that the sale takes place at the garden entrance (Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat 358:2).
and all of whom said 'hide it'. If one of these sellers told him to hide what he is buying, it is forbidden to buy from him.
the sharecropper. A person who works the field in place of the owner for a certain percentage of what grows in it.
women. Married ones.
minors. Who are supported at their father's table.
things that are presumed to be theirs with the owners' consent. Things that the owners presumably agreed would be theirs.
such as women who sold flax utensils in the Galilee or calves in the Sharon. For in those places these things are common and sold cheaply, so the owners are not particular about them.
oil pressers. Owners of olive presses who produce oil for other people.
by measure. If they sell them in a measured quantity.
the wool scraps that the launderer removes belong to him. Small pieces of wool left over after the launderer washes the wool to prepare it for use (Commentary to the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 10:10).
and that the carder. One who combs the wool as part of preparing it for weaving (ibid.).
the launderer takes three threads and they are his. If while washing the garment three threads were pulled out of it, the launderer may cut them off and take them (Meiri, Bava Kamma 119a).
if it was black on white, he takes all of it. If there are black threads on a white garment, the householder is not particular about their being taken, and the launderer may take them.
the tailor. Who received cloth to make a garment from it.
the length of the pull of a needle. Double the length of the needle (Commentary to the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 10:10).
a scrap. A piece of the garment.
the carpenter. The woodworker.
with the adze. A tool for fine smoothing of wood.
and with the plane. A tool for coarse smoothing of wood.
and if he was working at the householder's house etc.. For if he is a hired worker and did not take the work as a contractor, the householder is particular even about fine sawdust.
all these matters and the like follow the custom of the locality. Therefore these laws are not fixed but depend on what is customary in that place.
in the law of the locality. These laws that the Sages set according to local custom.
but one may buy from him a pillow full of wool scraps. Since a certain change was made to them by making them part of the pillow, the Sages permitted buying from him (Maggid Mishneh).
one who weighs for his fellow. What he is selling him and the like.
with deficient weights etc.. Weights whose weight is less than the standard, without the buyer's knowledge.
one who measures with a measure. A vessel for measuring volume.
even though the one who measures or weighs short is a thief. One who weighs or measures with a deficient weight or measure is considered a thief, because part of the payment he receives is not his.

he does not pay double payment. Some explain that the reason is that selling with a deficient weight or measure is robbery, and a robber is exempt from double payment (Maggid Mishneh). Others explained that this case is indeed more like theft, since part of the money was given because of deception, but he is exempt because the money was given with the buyer's knowledge, whereas the double payment applies when the stolen item was taken without the owner's knowledge (Even HaAzel).
rather he completes for him the measure or the weight. He must give the buyer the difference according to the full measure or weight.

and one is not flogged for this prohibition because he is liable to pay. He must return the difference, and there is a rule that one is not flogged for a prohibition that carries an obligation of payment (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).
anyone who keeps in his house etc.. Even if he does not use them.

you shall not have in your pouch. The continuation of the verse is 'a stone and a stone, large and small'; hence there is a prohibition against having deficient measures in one's possession even if they are lying in his pouch and not in use.
a chamber pot. A vessel for urine.
and one is not flogged for this prohibition because it involves no action. One is flogged for a transgression only when it involves an actual act (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1-2).
with a known seal. A defined and well-known marking.
it is permitted to keep them. For there is no concern that they will use them.
a sela. A coin with a defined weight that can also be used for weighing.
that was damaged. That was diminished.
and he should not throw it among his scrap metal. Lest he use it.
and he should not pierce it and hang it on his son's neck. He should not pierce it and use it as jewelry, even though he is not using it as a weight.
lest another come and make it a weight. And they will not notice the deficiency, since it is on the edge of the coin.
he should grind it. Crumble it.
he should cut it. Chop it up.
or throw it into the Dead Sea. In order to remove it from the world (the Dead Sea is the Great Sea, Hilchot Arachin vaCharamin 8:8 according to accurate versions).
if it was diminished down to half, he may keep it. At this amount there is no concern that people will err about it, so he may leave it with him.
if it was reduced to less than half, he should cut it up. Lest people err and take it to be a half-sela.

and if it was diminished by less than a sixth, he may keep it to do business with. A diminished coin can be put to two forbidden uses, payment and weighing. Deception in payment concerns the value of the item, and involves the prohibition of overcharging, not the prohibition of measures and weights. For the prohibition of weighing one transgresses with any amount, but the law of overcharging applies only when one misleads the other by a sixth (shtut), so he may keep a coin diminished by less than a sixth for payment (Hilchot Mekhirah 12:8-10).
for most people overlook anything less than a sixth in business dealings. See Hilchot Mekhirah 12:3.
or to a robber. A highway robber who does not kill.
because they deceive others with it. For they accept it from them for lack of choice even if it is not whole.
but he may pierce it and hang it on the child's neck. There is no concern that it will be used as a weight, since the defect is in the middle and the deception would be noticeable.
a sela damaged in the middle, it is forbidden to sell it. Even though the defect is noticeable.
to be killed. A robber who kills for the money.
a person makes his measures. The Sages enacted that one should make his measuring vessels with a noticeable difference between them.
a se'ah. It contains six kavs, and dry goods are measured with it.
and a quarter of a se'ah and a kav. A quarter of a se'ah is a kav and a half, and the ratio between a kav and it is two to three.
and half a rova. Half a quarter-kav.
and an eighth. A shemin.
so that it not be confused with a quarter of a se'ah, which is a kav and a half. For the ratio between them is three to four.
and likewise with liquid measures. Also for vessels measuring liquids, the Sages enacted that volumes be made with a noticeable difference between them.
a hin. Which contains twelve logs.

and they did not forbid making a third of a hin and a quarter of a hin etc.. Although the ratio between them is three to four, the Sages did not forbid making them since these measures were used in the Temple. In the Temple they did not forbid this because they relied on the priests not to confuse these measures (Bavli Bava Batra 90a).
in the days of Moses our teacher. For these measures were used for the libations, as explicitly stated in the Torah (Numbers chapter 15 and elsewhere, and see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 1:17).
whether one does business with a Jew or with a gentile who worships idols. See also above 1:1.
and likewise it is forbidden to mislead a gentile in calculation. When calculating sums of money with him, and not only in measures and weights (and compare Hilchot Gezelah vaAvedah 11:4-5).

and he shall reckon with his purchaser. This verse was said regarding a Jew who was sold into servitude to a gentile, where one of his relatives pays that purchaser to redeem him, and the redemption sum is set according to the number of years remaining until the Jubilee. From this we learn that the Jew must calculate precisely and is forbidden to deceive the gentile.
even though he is subdued under your hands. Even where Israel rules and imposes the laws of the Torah on the gentile regarding the redemption of a servant, it is forbidden to deceive the gentile.

and it says... in any case. This verse speaks about deception in weights and measures, and emphasizes that all deception is an abomination, regardless of whom one deceives (Commentary to the Mishnah, Kelim 12:7).
in surveying land. Measuring the land.

you shall not commit injustice in judgment, in measure etc.. The first part of the verse is a general command, 'you shall not commit injustice in judgment', and the second part specifies what the general command refers to: 'in measure, in weight, and in liquid measure'.
in the law of measure. A volume measure, as it says 'meshurah', which is a very small volume measure (below 8:7).
members of a group who are particular with one another. Who eat together from shared food, but are particular that each one take an equal share from it.
who exchanged a portion for a portion etc.. If they agreed that each would take a portion of the food, and in return the others would also take an equal amount.
or borrowed food from him and returned it to him. If one borrowed food from the other and they agreed that he would repay him an equal amount.

they transgress because of measure etc.. If for the exchange or the loan he weighed or counted the foods and was not exact in measuring, he transgresses these prohibitions because they are particular about it (based on Meiri, Bava Metzia 75a).
and because of lending and repaying on a festival. If they did so on a festival (see Hilchot Shabbat 23:12, Hilchot Yom Tov 4:19-21).
one who moves his fellow's boundary. He moved the boundary between the plots into the other's plot and thereby enlarged his own.
and this is between him and his fellow. Therefore repentance is not enough to atone for the sin; he must return to his fellow what he took from him and appease him (see Hilchot Teshuvah 2:9).
whoever denies the commandment of measures is like one who denies the exodus from Egypt. Which is mentioned at the end of the commandment of measures and weights (Leviticus 19:36).

for it is the beginning of the command. The exodus from Egypt is the basis of the obligation to keep the commandments, since on this condition God took us out of Egypt (Torat Kohanim, Kedoshim, parashah 3, chapter 8, halakhah 10).
for it caused all the commands. As a result of the exodus from Egypt we received all the commandments.
to be exact. To ensure that they are as precise as possible.
surveying the land. Measuring the land.
in the writings on geometry. Works on the science of mathematics.

that even a finger's breadth is regarded as if it were full of saffron. Even a very small area is treated as if it were sown with saffron, an expensive spice, and therefore one must be careful in measuring land.

the four cubits adjacent to a ditch are treated lightly in their measurement. A ditch is a water channel that passes between fields. The strip of land along its banks is not cultivated, so when measuring plots next to the channel one leaves a strip of four cubits and measures from there onward, but one need not be strict to measure a full four cubits (Rashi, Bava Metzia 107b; the Tosafot there explained the opposite, that one must be strict to measure a full four cubits).

and those adjacent to the bank of the river etc.. The four cubits on the riverbank serve the whole public, so one must be careful that the measuring begins only at a distance of four cubits from the river.

and one who measures the land. With a rope of a certain length, calculating the area by the number of times the rope fits along its length and width; and according to the number of ropes measured for the first, one also measures for the second.
with a reed or an iron chain and the like. Whose length is fixed.
it is of no consequence. There is no problem that they were used for measuring at different times of the year.
a bare rock. Hard stone.
and the like. That do not shrink.
the leveler. A kind of ruler that is passed over a measuring vessel to remove the excess quantity above the rim of the vessel.

not of gourd because it is lighter, and not of metal because it is heavier. Gourd is a light material, and when a gourd leveler is passed over the vessel it may not remove all the excess; with metal the concern is the opposite, that the leveler will sink into the cavity of the vessel because of its weight and remove some of what is inside the vessel.
but he may make one of olive wood or nut wood etc.. From these woods, whose weight is moderate.
the leveler is not made etc.. So that its measure be uniform and the leveling too be uniform.
short. Thin.
and he should not level little by little because he reduces it for the seller. If he passes the leveler in several strokes, he may not remove all the excess.
and he should not level all at once because he reduces it for the buyer. When he passes the leveler in one quick motion, he may also remove some of what is inside the vessel.
one does not bury weights in salt. Because the salt corrodes the weights.
and he should not make it foam in a liquid measure. He should not pour liquid into a measuring vessel in a way that creates foam.
even if the measure is very small. Although he pours into a small vessel and with a small pour there is hardly any foam.
a small measure, one thirty-third of a log. A measure with a volume of about ten milliliters.
iron lumps. Lumps of raw iron, which are very heavy.

the beam of the scale must be etc.. The coarser and heavier the item being weighed, the larger the scale needed so that the scale's operation not be disrupted; and the finer and lighter it is, the smaller the scale needed so that it can show small differences (and see also Hilchot Kelim 21:5).
the cord of the scale... hangs in the air three handbreadths. The cord that holds between his hand and the beam of the scale shall be three handbreadths long.
and they are three handbreadths above the ground. The pans of the scale must be at least three handbreadths above the ground.
the beam of the scale. The balanced part of the scale, on which the weights are hung.
the scales of wool sellers and glass sellers. Who sell smaller weights.
a shopkeeper's scales. Who sells small quantities.
the pelles. A type of scale (perhaps this refers to the scale of a money changer, with which he weighs coins; see Rabbi Yosef ibn Migash, Bava Batra 89a).
fine purple. Wool dyed purple, which is expensive, so people are careful about its weight.
three fingers. Which is three quarters of a handbreadth.
and the length of the pelles. The beam of the scale.
the chains. The cords on which the weights are hung.
as much as he wants. The Sages did not set a measure for this.

from where do we know that the seller must give extra weight... a perfect and just stone you shall have. The verse mentions the obligation to weigh with a perfect stone and also the obligation of justice, and from this we learn that it is not enough for the weight to be balanced, but it must also tip in the buyer's favor.
from your own. At your expense.
and how much. What is the amount the Sages set for this.
in liquids. Fluids.

in liquids one in a hundred, and in dry goods one in four hundred. In liquids one must tip by a greater proportion because some clings to the vessel from which he transfers it to the buyer, and the buyer receives less (Rashbam, Bava Batra 88b).
ratals. A unit of weight, the same as the litra mentioned shortly after (Commentary to the Mishnah, Terumot 4:10).
additions. The extra that the seller adds.
one tenth of a litra. A tenth of a litra out of the total of ten litras, which is one percent of them.
whether a large or a small amount. Whether he is weighing something of great or small weight.
eye to eye. To weigh in a balanced manner.
but in a place where they were accustomed to give extra weight. To add of the merchandise to the pan until it is lower than the opposite pan.
he must give him extra weight of a handbreadth. He adds until the pan is a handbreadth lower than the other pan.

he may not say to him: weigh one by one and give extra weight. The buyer cannot demand that he weigh each litra separately, even though in any case the seller adds one percent or tips by a handbreadth, because in every tipping a little more than the tip is always added, and this causes the seller a loss.

a place where they were accustomed to measure with a small measure etc.. If they customarily used a small measuring vessel, he may not use a large vessel but must measure with the small vessel several times, and likewise the reverse. Since one cannot be exact in the addition he is obliged to give, the number of measurings affects the addition and the final quantity, and therefore one should not deviate from the local custom (Maggid Mishneh).
to level. To remove the excess quantity beyond the cavity of the measuring vessel.

to level, he may not heap it and add to the price etc.. Even if he settles accounts with him for it, he may not change the customary manner of measuring. The Sages learned this from the verse 'a just ephah you shall have' (Bavli Bava Batra 89a).
to add to the measures or the weights. To change the system of measures and enlarge it by a certain percentage.
a sixth. A shtut.
the wholesaler. One who buys large quantities of food and drink and sells them to shopkeepers.
wipes. Cleans.
and the householder. Who sells only from time to time.
and the shopkeeper. The owner of a store who sells a lot in small quantities.
on Shabbat. Meaning, in the week.
and washes. Rinses with water.
after each and every weighing. After each weighing of a wet item (Shulchan Aruch).
so that they not rust. That the Sages permitted making scales out of metal (unlike weights, above halakhah 5), provided he takes care that they are dry.
one who wants to weigh three quarters of a litra. A buyer who wants to buy something such as meat, weighing three quarters of a litra.
for if you say he puts half a litra and a quarter of a litra in one pan. This is a simpler way, in which he weighs the meat alone against two weights totaling three quarters of a litra.

lest the quarter litra fall and the buyer not see it. And he would give him meat weighing half a litra. But when he puts the quarter litra together with the meat against the weight of a litra, the seller himself will take care that the quarter-litra weight not fall, so as not to weigh him a litra of meat for payment of three quarters of a litra.
the court is obligated to appoint officers etc.. See Hilchot Sanhedrin 1:1-2, Hilchot Mekhirah 14:1-2, 14:9-11 (where additional regulations of the townspeople in matters of commerce appear).
in every province... and in every district. In every city and in every region.
they go around to the shops. They go around among the stores.
and they set the prices. They set the maximum price for each commodity.
to strike him according to his strength. According to his ability to absorb lashes.
a warning for kidnapping. Whereas the prohibition of stealing money is learned from the verse 'you shall not steal' (Leviticus 19:11, above 1:1).

because it is a prohibition given as a warning for a death penalty of the court. For the main thrust of the prohibition concerns the death penalty and not flogging, so one is not flogged for it (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).
as it says: if a man is found kidnapping a person. And later in the verse it says 'and that thief shall die'.
an Israelite. A person from Israel (see below 9:6).
and brings him into his domain. Into the thief's domain.
and treated him as a slave. The Sages interpreted this to mean making use of him.
even if he used him only for less than the value of a perutah. Even if the value of the use does not reach a perutah.
even if the kidnapped person was asleep. And did not serve the thief consciously and actively.
or he sold him before using him. That he sold him and did not use him (Meiri, Sanhedrin 85b).
and likewise if he kidnapped him while he was asleep... he is exempt. Only if he was awake at one of these stages is he liable.
he stipulated with the buyer. He made a condition with the buyer.
this maidservant. A term for a woman whom he kidnapped and made his maidservant.

he is exempt. Since the fetus is considered asleep, and this is like kidnapping a sleeping person, for which one is exempt (Aruch LaNer, Sanhedrin 85b, and Yad Pashut; and see Meiri and Minchat Chinuch, commandment 36, who explained in other ways).

guardians who kidnapped the orphans who are in their care. Guardians who kidnapped the orphans they take care of. [Note: the vocalization of the word 'apitropin' follows the Greek source. In the Commentary to the Mishnah in the Rambam's own handwriting this word appears in several vocalizations: sometimes the first pe is vocalized with a kubutz, sometimes with a patach (and in some places the pe has no vowel).]
those who are supported at his table. Who eat from his food.
as it says: and he is found in his hand. This implies that the kidnapping made him available in his hand, and before that he was not available in his hand.
available in his hand. Common with him.
a day-old infant whose months were completed. Who was born after nine months of pregnancy and is not suspected of being a stillborn (see Hilchot Rotzeach 2:6).
a kidnapper in every case. Anyone who kidnaps is liable, and for every person kidnapped they are liable.
and these are included among our brothers in the Torah and the commandments. And they are called brothers even though they were not born Jews.

one who is half slave and half free is exempt. A Canaanite slave who belonged to two partners and one of them freed him. Since a Canaanite slave is not obligated in all the commandments like a Jew, one is exempt for selling him.
one who comes in through a tunnel. Who enters a house through a breach or a dug opening to steal.
he has no blood. There is no prohibition of shedding his blood.

and everyone has permission to kill him etc.. His law is not that of someone liable to a court-ordered death, where the court is responsible for killing him by the type of death that depends on the offense he committed, and the court also does not carry out death penalties on Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 24:7); rather he is like one who pursues his fellow to kill him, whom one may kill by any means (Hilchot Rotzeach 1:6, and see below 9:9 in Piskim veShitot).
by any death. By any manner of killing.
his enclosure. An area surrounded by partitions, meant for various uses.
even though he came for matters of money. That he came to steal and not to kill, and a thief is not punished by death.
since it is presumed. That presumably he will kill the householder if he tries to prevent him from stealing.
whether he was a minor. Since he endangers the owner, even though he is not subject to punishment.
that this thief who came upon him will not kill him. If he tries to prevent him from stealing.
he has killed a person, as it says: if the sun has risen upon him. And the continuation of the verse is 'there is blood for him', meaning that one who kills him is considered to have shed blood.
for certainly he will not kill him. Because it is the way of a father to have great mercy on his son.
but a son who comes upon his father is killed. For he may kill him.
and found him and he left the tunnel. When he discovered him he left the tunnel.
he has blood. And it is forbidden to kill him.
and likewise if witnesses or people surrounded him etc.. For in these situations there is no expected danger to the owners.
the pen and the enclosure. Places where flocks are gathered.
any thief who has blood. And it is forbidden to kill him.
if a stone pile fell on him on Shabbat, one clears it off him. One clears away a collapse that fell on him, out of concern that he will die (see Hilchot Shabbat 2:18).
but one who has no blood. And may be killed.

that he broke utensils on entering is exempt, as we have explained. Above 3:1, that he does not incur monetary payment for an act for which he is liable to death (and see also Hilchot Chovel uMazik 8:12).
